setting: a coastal wind turbine installer evaluating a remote monitoring dashboard (Zephyr Harbor)
prompt: I need a quick stress test of the remote monitoring dashboard proposal for Zephyr Harbor before I present it to our COO, Maya Patel, on Thursday, 2025‑07‑01. We’re looking at a $2.3 million upfront investment, with a rollout timeline of 12 months and an expected 85 % uptime in the first year. The business case assumes the existing SCADA platform can integrate via a standard API at no extra cost, and we’ve priced the annual bandwidth and maintenance increase at 5 % of the license fee. The projected ROI is $1.2 million after 12 months, which we’re comparing to a competitor’s solution that claims a 3‑year ROI of $3.5 million, but we haven’t adjusted for the fact that their system includes hardware that we would need to buy separately. The unknown we can’t quantify yet is the latency of the satellite link in bad weather, which could affect real‑time alerts. Please give me: (1) a clear recommendation on whether to move forward, (2) the three most likely ways this rollout could fail, and (3) the specific result or metric that would trigger us to kill the project or pivot to an alternative.

setting: a family‑run bakery in Oaxaca weighing a nationwide delivery network (Masa Trail)
prompt: I’m pulling together the pitch for Carlos, the owner, to get his sign‑off on launching a nationwide delivery network for our Masa Trail line. The plan calls for buying 12 insulated vans at $12,500 each (total $150,000) and leasing a central hub warehouse for $3,500 per month starting 1 July 2024. We estimate we can handle 2,000 orders per month after the first quarter, with an average order value of $23 and a 3% net margin. My assumption is that demand will grow 15% each quarter and that fuel prices will stay flat for the next 12 months. The unknown is how many customers in Mexico City and Monterrey will actually try the service within the first three months—no market test yet. I need one clear recommendation: go ahead, delay, or re‑scope. Also list the three biggest ways this could fail (e.g., logistics bottlenecks, spoilage, cost overruns). Finally, specify the result that would trigger us to kill the project or pivot—like if cumulative net loss exceeds $35,000 by 30 June 2025. Let me know if any of the figures look off, especially the total capital outlay.

setting: a startup fintech hub in Nairobi assessing a micro‑loan chatbot (Cobalt Ledger)
prompt: I’m drafting the go‑ahead pitch for Cobalt Ledger, our AI‑driven micro‑loan chatbot, to present to Maya Patel, our COO, next Thursday. The plan assumes we’ll launch in Q3 2025 and immediately handle about 30,000 chat interactions per month, each costing $0.05 in processing fees, giving us $1,500 monthly (or $18,000 annually) in direct costs. We project a conversion rate of 80 % from chat to approved loan, meaning roughly 24,000 loans a month at an average size of $150, which would generate $3.6 million in disbursements monthly. Development is budgeted at $120,000, and we’ve allocated $45,000 for the first three months of marketing, assuming a customer‑acquisition cost of $10 per loan. The competitor’s API‑only solution charges $0.03 per transaction, but we’re not counting their integration overhead. The unknown is the regulatory approval timeline – the central bank could take anywhere from 2 to 8 months. I need you to give me: one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, the three most likely ways this rollout could fail, and the specific metric or event that would trigger us to stop or pivot the project.

setting: a mid‑size dairy cooperative in Wisconsin weighing a plant‑based product line (Creamy Forge)
prompt: I’m the head of new product development at Northbrook Dairy Cooperative in Wisconsin and I need a quick stress‑test of our “Creamy Forge” plant‑based line before I present it to our CEO, Marjorie Patel, next week. We plan to spend $3.2 million on equipment (install by 30 Jun 2025) and $450 k per year on additional utilities. The business case projects $5 million in revenue by FY 2026, a 15 % gross margin, and a 12 % share of the regional plant‑based market after 18 months. The assumption is that our existing distribution network can absorb an extra 2,000 pallets per month without new contracts. The pilot will run from 1 Jan 2025 to 31 Mar 2025 with a target of 10,000 units per month; we’ll need to price at $4.99 to hit the margin. One unknown is how our core dairy customers will react to us selling a non‑dairy product under the same brand. Also, the break‑even estimate says we’ll recover the CAPEX in 10 months, but I’m not sure the calculation includes the $250 k marketing spend we’ve allocated. Please give me one clear recommendation, outline the main ways this could fail, and tell me the specific result (e.g., volume or margin shortfall) that would trigger us to cancel or re‑scope the project.

setting: a boutique travel agency in Reykjavik considering a virtual reality itinerary planner (Glacier Pulse)
prompt: I’m preparing a briefing for our CEO, Jón, about whether we should move forward with the Glacier Pulse virtual‑reality itinerary planner for our boutique Reykjavik agency. We’ve run a pilot with three of our most popular tours (Golden Circle, Blue Lagoon, and the Northern Lights chase) over the past two months, and the pilot showed a 12 % lift in bookings among participants, which we’re estimating could translate to roughly $250 k in extra revenue per year if the trend holds. The development budget we’ve been quoted is $250 k, with an expected rollout in Q4 2025 after a six‑month build phase. We’re assuming 70 % of our existing client base will adopt the VR planner once it’s live, but we have no hard data on that adoption rate and we haven’t priced the licensing fees Glacier Pulse will charge (the unknown). Also, we haven’t included any cost for integrating the VR module with our current booking engine, which could add another $50 k. I need you to give Jón one clear recommendation, outline the three biggest ways this project could fail, and tell me the specific metric (e.g., less than 5 % adoption after three months) that would trigger us to kill the initiative.

setting: a public university research department in Helsinki weighing a partnership with a biotech incubator (Nordic Helix)
prompt: I’m the director of the Molecular Imaging Unit at Helsinki University of Technology, and I need a stress‑test of the partnership proposal we’re about to present to Dr. Leena Koskinen, our Vice President of Research. We have a €2.4 million budget earmarked for the next 18 months, and the plan assumes that Nordic Helix’s CRISPR‑based gene‑editing platform will reach GMP‑grade production by month 12. We would allocate 12 of our post‑docs and technicians, split the overhead 50/50, and expect joint publications to generate €1.2 million in external grant revenue over three years. The incubator claims a 30 % faster time‑to‑market than any local competitor, but we have no hard data on their actual success rate. The unknown here is the EU regulatory approval timeline for the first clinical trial, which could add anywhere from 6 to 18 months. Also, we have double‑counted the €300 k equipment grant we already receive from the city, inflating the projected cash‑flow. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, outline the main ways this collaboration could fail, and specify the trigger condition (e.g., if regulatory approval exceeds 12 months) that would make us abort or pivot.

setting: a senior care home chain in Queensland assessing a robot‑assisted medication system (Grove Sentinel)
prompt: I'm preparing a proposal for the board chair, Ms. Lila Hart, to adopt the Grove Sentinel robot‑assisted medication system across our senior care homes in Queensland. We have 12 facilities, each with an average of 78 residents. The vendor quotes $1.2 million for a pilot in three sites for 6 months, plus $250k per additional site per year. We assume the robot will reduce medication errors by 30% based on a study at a US nursing chain with 1500 beds, but we haven't factored staff training time. Our current error rate is 2.8% per month, costing us $45,000 in penalties annually. The pilot would start on 1 November 2024 and run until 30 April 2025. I need you to give Ms. Hart one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, list the top three ways the rollout could fail, and tell me the specific metric that, if it rises above 1.5% error rate by the end of the pilot, should trigger us to kill the project. Also note any hidden cost or risk you see that we might have missed.

setting: a small‑batch craft brewery in Dublin weighing a carbon‑offset subscription (Emerald Hops)
prompt: I’m Mike, the operations lead at Celtic Brew Co., and I need a quick stress‑test before I bring this to Siobhan O’Leary, our Chief Sustainability Officer. We’re looking at a 12‑month carbon‑offset subscription from Emerald Hops that costs €2,500 per month and claims to offset 12 tCO₂ annually. Our current emissions, based on the 2023 audit, are 45 tCO₂ per year, and we have a board‑approved target to cut net emissions by 30 % by the end of 2025. The plan would run a trial for 18 months, after which we would decide whether to roll it into the budget. I’m assuming the EU carbon price stays at €25 per tonne, so the offset would “save” us €300 k in avoided tax over the next three years. The unknown is how the new Irish brewery emissions cap, expected to be announced in Q3 2025, will affect our compliance obligations. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, list the main ways this could fail (including any hidden costs or risks), and specify the result that would trigger us to stop or change course (e.g., if net reduction falls below a certain threshold).

setting: a municipal water utility in Mendoza evaluating a smart‑meter rollout (Aqua Ember)
prompt: I need you to stress‑test the smart‑meter rollout proposal for Aqua Ember before I present it to our COO, Maria Torres, next Thursday. We plan to install 250,000 meters across the city over a three‑year period (2025‑2027) with a $12 million capital budget. The business case assumes a 90 % household adoption rate and projects an 8 % reduction in water loss, which we estimate will save $1.2 million annually – roughly 15 % of the upfront cost (I realize the arithmetic is off, but that’s the figure the finance team used). We are also assuming the existing SCADA system can ingest the data without additional hardware; the real unknown is the integration cost, which the vendor has not quantified. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, the three biggest ways this could fail (technical, financial, or regulatory), and the specific result that would trigger us to halt the program or pivot (e.g., if the first‑year adoption falls below 60 %). Also flag any hidden risk or cost we haven’t considered.

setting: a fast‑fashion retailer in Manila considering a recycled‑fabric line (Silk Mirage)
prompt: I need a quick stress‑test of the “Silk Mirage” recycled‑fabric line before I pitch it to our CEO, Maya Torres, next week. We have a $2.2 million upfront budget (including $600k for equipment, $400k for initial raw‑material contracts, and $200k for a pilot marketing splash). The finance team projects $4.5 million in sales in the first 12 months, which they say would give us a 12% margin and $1.5 million profit. Our timeline is to start production by 15 July 2025 and hit stores across Manila by 1 Oct 2025. I’m assuming the supplier in Cebu can reliably deliver 150,000 meters of recycled polyester per month at the quoted $3.30 per meter. The unknowns are the actual consumer price elasticity for eco‑friendly apparel and the precise carbon‑offset credit value we could claim. Please give me one clear recommendation (go/not go), list the three biggest ways this plan could fail, and tell me the pre‑agreed trigger that would make us stop or pivot (e.g., if a metric falls below a threshold). Also note any hidden cost or arithmetic error you see in the numbers I’ve given.

setting: a nonprofit wildlife reserve in Zambia weighing an eco‑tourism platform (Savanna Whisper)
prompt: I’m drafting a briefing for Dr. Lila Moyo, our CEO, about launching the Savanna Whisper eco‑tourism platform. We have a $180,000 seed budget approved for Q3 2025, and a three‑year technology contract that costs $45,000 per year. The plan projects 12,000 visitors in year 1, rising to 15,000 by year 3, which we say is a 30 % increase over our current 11,500 annual visitors. We assume 70 % of those guests will book directly through Savanna Whisper, paying a 12 % commission that should generate $216,000 in gross revenue in the first year. The target breakeven point is $180,000 plus the $45,000 annual tech fee, but the arithmetic was presented as $210,000 total cost, not $225,000. We also expect a modest $5,000 marketing spend each quarter and have not priced the unknown regulatory fee for foreign operators, which could be up to $20,000 annually. I need you to give me one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, list the main ways the initiative could fail, and tell me the specific result (e.g., revenue below $180,000 after six months) that would trigger us to kill or pivot the project.

setting: a corporate law firm in Toronto assessing an AI contract review tool (Lexi Forge)
prompt: I’m drafting a proposal to present to our managing partner, Sarah Patel, about adopting Lexi Forge, an AI contract review tool, and I need it stress‑tested before the board meeting on 12 November 2026. Our firm handles roughly 1,200 contracts per month, and the pilot we ran in March–May processed 150 agreements at an average of 45 minutes each, down from the baseline of 65 minutes, which we reported as a 30 % time savings. The vendor charges a subscription of $9,500 per month plus a one‑time integration fee of $42,000, and we estimate a labor cost reduction of $78,000 per quarter. I’m assuming the AI’s clause‑identification accuracy will stay at least 92 % as advertised, but the false‑negative rate for indemnity clauses is unknown. We also haven’t priced the internal training time, which we roughly estimate at 40 hours at $250 per hour. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, outline the primary ways this rollout could fail (including any hidden costs or performance gaps), and specify the concrete result—e.g., a month‑over‑month cost‑savings below $15,000 for three consecutive months—that would trigger us to halt or re‑evaluate the project.

setting: a regional airline in Kenya weighing a fuel‑efficiency retrofit program (Nimbus Wings)
prompt: I’m the VP of Operations at Azure Skies, a regional airline that flies 12 Cessna 208B Grand Caravans across Kenya’s domestic network. We are looking at the Nimbus Wings retrofit, which vendor AeroTech says will reduce fuel burn by 7.5% per flight. The quoted retrofit cost is $48,000 per aircraft, and we estimate a payback in 2.8 years based on our current fuel consumption of 1,200 liters per flight at $0.96 per liter, 150 flights per month per plane. I am assuming fuel price will stay within ±5% of today’s rate for the next three years. The unknown is the real‑world failure rate of the wing extensions in high‑temperature, dusty runway conditions; AeroTech only provides data from a temperate European fleet. Also, the cost spreadsheet we received mistakenly adds $240,000 to the total program cost, double‑counting the first three aircraft. I need a brief for our CEO, Lila Mwangi, that includes one clear recommendation, the three biggest ways the retrofit could fail, and the specific metric—if the actual fuel savings fall below 4% after the first 12 months—that would trigger us to kill the project. Please also note any hidden risk you spot.

setting: a cloud‑gaming startup in Seoul evaluating a server‑less infrastructure (Pixel Rift)
prompt: Jin Park, our CEO, wants a go‑no‑go on moving Pixel Rift to a fully server‑less stack before the Q4 launch on 2024‑12‑01. I need you to stress‑test the proposal. We’ve run a pilot on 150 concurrent sessions and measured an average latency of 15 ms, which meets our internal target of ≤20 ms (assumption: 20 ms is sufficient for player satisfaction). The pilot cost $2.3 M in compute and storage, but we excluded network egress, which the cloud provider estimates at $0.12 per GB; with an expected 5 PB of monthly traffic, that could add $600 k. Our forecast is 500 k users in the first six months, with 12 % converting to the premium tier—though we have no real data on churn for that tier (unknown). We also compared the server‑less price to our current on‑prem solution using average load, not peak spikes, which could understate costs. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, outline the three biggest ways this could fail (technical, financial, or market), and specify the result—e.g., sustained latency >25 ms or monthly cost >$4 M—that would make us stop or pivot.

setting: a heritage book publisher in Edinburgh weighing a print‑on‑demand service (Inkspire Quill)
prompt: I’m drafting a proposal for Fiona MacLeod, our Chief Publishing Officer, about moving a portion of our back‑list titles to Inkspire Quill’s print‑on‑demand (POD) service. Right now we print 150,000 copies annually at £5.50 each and pay a £12,000 monthly warehouse lease. Inkspire charges £4.90 per copy plus a £2,500 set‑up fee per title; we plan a six‑month integration and a pilot with three titles, each expected to sell 10,000 copies a year. We assume demand will stay flat and that our current paper‑supplier discount will stay unchanged. The arithmetic we ran suggests we’d save about £10,500 in variable printing costs, but we haven’t priced the extra shipping cost per POD unit (unknown) nor the IT integration effort we estimate at £8,000. We also assume POD quality will match our existing print quality, which hasn’t been validated. I need you to give me one clear recommendation for Fiona, list the main ways this rollout could fail, and tell me the specific result that would make us stop or change course (for example, if total per‑unit cost rises above £5.75 or inventory turnover drops below 1.5).

setting: a municipal waste management department in Lisbon assessing autonomous collection trucks (Terra Pulse)
prompt: I'm preparing a brief for our director, Maria Silva, on whether to move forward with a pilot of Terra Pulse autonomous collection trucks for the Lisbon Waste Management Department. We have a budget of €8 million for 2025, and the vendor quoted €1.2 million per unit, promising a 20 % reduction in fuel use and a 15 % cut in labor costs. We currently operate 45 diesel trucks at €50 k annual maintenance each; the pilot would replace 12 of them starting 2025‑03‑01 for a six‑month trial. The proposal assumes the city’s street‑level 3D map will be completed by Q2 2025, and that the autonomous software will integrate with our existing routing system without additional licensing fees. The unknown is the actual downtime we’ll experience due to software glitches and sensor failures, which the vendor has not quantified. I need you to give me one clear recommendation on whether to approve the pilot, outline the three biggest ways this could fail (technical, regulatory, financial), and specify the pre‑agreed condition that would trigger us to cancel the program (e.g., if total operational cost exceeds €1.5 million per month). Include any glaring oversights you spot, such as missing insurance costs or the arithmetic mismatch between the total vehicle cost and our allocated budget.

setting: a boutique architecture studio in Portland weighing a modular housing project (Stone Loom)
prompt: I’m the senior project lead at Loomline Studios, a boutique architecture shop in Portland, and I’m preparing to brief our founder Maya Patel on the Stone Loom modular housing proposal. We have secured $5.2 million in seed funding (assumed to cover design, permits and the first 12 months of production). The plan is to fabricate 12 units a month at $92,000 each, ship them to the site, and finish interiors on‑site. At that rate we expect to break even after 18 months and generate roughly $30 million in sales over four years (the calculation assumes 12 units × $92k × 24 months = $26.5 M plus 10 % margin). We’re counting on the city approving the new mixed‑use zoning within 90 days, and we’ve budgeted a 3 % annual inflation buffer. The unknown is the final toll rate for the new highway loop that will be the primary transport corridor; the agency has not released the fee schedule yet. I need you to give Maya one clear recommendation, outline the three biggest ways this project could fail, and state the specific condition (e.g., transport cost exceeding X% of unit price) that would trigger us to cancel or redesign the plan.

setting: a high‑school robotics club in Bangalore considering a sponsorship from a drone maker (Aero Sparks)
prompt: I’m the club lead for the North Bangalore High‑School Robotics Team and I need to run a plan past our principal, Ms. Meera, before I bring it to the school board. Aero Sparks has offered to sponsor us with two DJI‑type drones priced at $7,500 each, plus a $1,500 training package, so the total outlay would be $16,500. Our current annual budget is $15,000, and we would have to reallocate $1,500 from the upcoming competition travel fund (we have 24 members and plan to attend the National Robotics Challenge on 12 Dec 2024 and the State Expo on 30 Mar 2025). Aero Sparks wants their logo on our team shirts for the next three months and a mention in all press releases. I’m assuming the drones will boost our win probability by 20 % based on their specs, but I have no data on how they perform in Bangalore’s high‑heat summer, nor on any hidden insurance or import duties. Could you give me a single recommendation on whether to accept the sponsorship, outline the three biggest ways this could fail, and tell me what specific result (e.g., a single crash or a regulatory ban) would trigger us to drop the deal? The answer is for Ms. Meera and the school board.

setting: a specialty tea importer in Marrakech weighing a direct‑to‑consumer subscription (Marrakeg Leaf)
prompt: I’m drafting a proposal to take Marrakeg Leaf, our direct‑to‑consumer tea subscription, to our CFO, Claire Dupont, next week. I’ve crunched the numbers: we’d charge $35 per month, aim for 1,500 subscribers by the end of the first year, and allocate a $30,000 marketing budget to acquire them. The cost per box is $2 for packaging plus $5 for shipping, and I’ve added a 7% customs duty on the tea leaf itself, which I estimate at $1 per box. I’m assuming that 30% of our current wholesale customers will stay on board and not switch to the subscription, so the loss of wholesale volume will be limited to $12,000 annually. The launch is slated for June 1 2024, with a three‑month pilot to test logistics. The real unknown is the churn rate for subscription customers after the first three months. I need you to give me one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, outline the main ways this plan could fail (including any hidden costs or risks you spot), and specify the result that would trigger us to kill or pivot the project (e.g., a specific churn threshold or cost overrun).

setting: a regional health clinic in Alberta evaluating a tele‑medicine platform (Prairie Echo)
prompt: I’m drafting a brief for Dr. Maya Patel, our medical director, about adopting the Prairie Echo tele‑medicine platform at the Northway Regional Clinic. We currently see about 250 patients per month for chronic‑care follow‑ups, and the platform charges $12,000 per quarter. The contract promises a 95 % system uptime, but our on‑site EMR has a 99 % uptime. We assume the average in‑person visit costs $150, so a virtual visit at $30 would save $120 per encounter, but we haven’t factored the $3,800 per‑year training budget we estimated for staff. The platform also claims it can reduce no‑show rates by 3 % (from 12 % down to 9 %). One unknown is the exact integration cost with our existing Epic‑Lite EMR, which the vendor says “will be minimal.” I need you to give me one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, outline the three biggest ways this rollout could fail, and specify the trigger that would make us stop or pivot – for example, if after three months the average patient satisfaction score falls below 80 % or the total quarterly cost exceeds $15,000. Please keep the analysis tight and flag any hidden risks.
